questions.question: In a desert, mice eat seeds, snakes eat the mice, and owls swoop down on the snakes. Ecologists sort the eaters in a food chain like this one into levels of consumers, counted up from the plants. At which consumer level is the owl in this chain?
choices: Primary consumer
Secondary consumer
Tertiary consumer
Quaternary consumer
questions.context: The seeds come from producers, the first level. The mice that eat them are primary consumers, the snakes that eat the mice are secondary consumers, and the owls that eat the snakes are tertiary consumers, at the fourth level. A quaternary consumer would be a fifth level, an animal that hunts the owls.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade ecology names the trophic levels, from producers through primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, and asks students to place the members of a chain on them.

questions.question: A camper eats a handful of wild berries for lunch. For supper he cooks a rabbit he caught, and rabbits eat only plants. At what feeding level is the camper in each of his two meals?
choices: Primary consumer, then secondary consumer
Primary consumer at both meals
Secondary consumer at both meals
Secondary consumer, then tertiary consumer
questions.context: Eating berries, which are part of a plant, the camper feeds as a primary consumer; eating a plant-eater, he feeds one level higher, as a secondary consumer. People are omnivores, and an omnivore can feed at more than one level from one meal to the next, which is one reason a real food web is untidier than a neat chain.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade applies the trophic levels to omnivores, which feed at more than one level.

questions.question: A wild rabbit nibbles grass for much of the day, and its body absorbs energy from everything it eats. Over the rabbit's whole life, where does most of that absorbed energy end up?
questions.answer: Used for living, then given off as heat
choices: Used for living, then given off as heat
Stored in its body until a fox eats it
Passed back to the grass through the soil
Turned into matter as the rabbit grows
questions.context: A warm-blooded animal spends nearly all the energy it absorbs on living: moving, breathing, mending its body and keeping warm, and that energy ends up as heat given off to its surroundings. Less than a tenth of it is built into the body, where a fox could get it. Grass takes its energy from sunlight, never from the soil, and energy is not turned into matter.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards explain the shrinking energy pyramid by the energy each level uses for living and loses as heat.

questions.question: In a meadow, rabbits eat the grass and foxes eat the rabbits. Ecologists use a rough rule of thumb: about a tenth of the energy at one feeding level reaches the next level up. By that rule, about what share of the grass's energy reaches the foxes?
choices: About a tenth
About a hundredth
About a thousandth
About a fifth
questions.context: About a tenth of the grass's energy reaches the rabbits, and a tenth of that, a tenth of a tenth, reaches the foxes: about a hundredth. The shares multiply at each step rather than add up, so it is not a fifth. The tenth is only a rough guide, since measured shares often run from about a twentieth to a fifth.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade uses the rough ten percent rule to describe how the energy available shrinks at each level of an energy pyramid.

questions.question: A single oak tree can feed about 2,000 leaf-eating insects, and those insects feed a much smaller number of birds. Counted by number of living things, the oak's level is the smallest of the three. In an energy pyramid of this food chain, which level is widest?
choices: The tree
The insects
The birds
All three alike
questions.context: All the energy the insects and the birds get comes from the oak, and most of it is used for living and lost as heat at each step, so the tree's level holds the most energy. A pyramid of numbers can stand on its point when one big producer feeds many small eaters, but a pyramid of energy is never upside down.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade reads and builds energy pyramids, which always narrow upward from the producers.

questions.question: Suppose two kinds of hunting bird, alike in size and appetite, share a big marsh. One kind lives by catching mice, which eat seeds. The other lives by catching frogs, which eat insects that feed on plants. If food alone sets their numbers, which kind can the marsh feed more of?
questions.answer: The mouse-catchers, as mice eat plants
choices: The mouse-catchers, as mice eat plants
The frog-catchers, as frogs eat animals
The same number, as the birds are alike in size
The same number, as both kinds of bird eat meat
questions.context: The mouse-catchers feed one level nearer the plants, so more of the plants' energy is left by the time it reaches them. Each step up a food chain leaves less energy, which is why top predators are always far fewer than the plant-eaters below them. Eating meat-eating prey does not give a hunter more energy; it puts the hunter a level higher, where there is less.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade uses the energy pyramid to explain why top predators are few and why more animals can live lower on a food chain.

questions.question: Most food chains in nature have only four or five levels, from the plants up to a top predator, and few run any longer than that. What keeps food chains so short?
questions.answer: Too little energy is left to feed another level
choices: Too little energy is left to feed another level
Each level destroys most of the energy it eats
The atoms in food are used up along the way
The top predators hold most of the energy
questions.context: So much energy is used for living and lost as heat at each step that after four or five levels there is too little left to support another. The energy is not destroyed, since it becomes heat, and the atoms in food are not used up but cycle back to the soil and air. Ecologists add that chains run longer in rich, settled places with plenty of plant growth, so energy is the main reason but not the whole story.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade ecology explains why food chains rarely run past four or five levels by the energy lost at each step.

questions.question: A carbon atom in a blade of grass passes to a rabbit that eats the grass, then to a fox that eats the rabbit, carried along with some of the food's energy. When the fox dies, fungi and bacteria break its body down. Which of the two can new grass use again?
questions.answer: The atom, but not the energy
choices: The atom, but not the energy
The energy, but not the atom
Both the atom and the energy
Neither the atom nor the energy
questions.context: Decomposers return the fox's carbon to the air as carbon dioxide, and grass can take it in again, so matter cycles round and round. Energy does not: at every step it is used for living and leaves as heat, which no plant can use to make food. That is why every food chain needs a fresh supply of energy from sunlight, while its matter is used again and again.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards contrast matter, which cycles through an ecosystem, with energy, which flows through it and out.

questions.question: Fungi and bacteria are a forest's main decomposers. Yet when ecologists number the feeding levels of the forest's food chains, from the plants up to the top predators, they usually leave the decomposers out. Why do they leave them out?
questions.answer: They feed on dead matter from every level
choices: They feed on dead matter from every level
They make their own food, as plants do
They hold too little energy to be counted
They take in no energy from what they eat
questions.context: Decomposers feed on dead plants, droppings and dead animals from every level, the top predators included, so they fit no single step of the chain. They take in a great deal of energy: on land most plant growth is never eaten by animals, and when it dies it goes to the decomposers. The fungi and bacteria that work as decomposers cannot make their own food as plants do.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade places decomposers in the flow of energy and matter, feeding on the remains of every level.

questions.question: On a grassland, grasshoppers eat the grass, songbirds eat the grasshoppers, and hawks eat the songbirds. Suppose an ecologist could weigh every living thing at each of these four levels, all together. Which level's total weight would be the smallest?
choices: The hawks
The songbirds
The grasshoppers
The grass
questions.context: Each level up holds less energy, and so less living matter: the grass outweighs the grasshoppers, the grasshoppers outweigh the birds that eat them, and the hawks weigh least of all. One grasshopper is tiny, but there are so many that together they far outweigh the few birds that hunt them.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade uses the pyramid of feeding levels to predict that the top level holds the least living matter and the fewest predators.
